turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Nice to meet you. Um, so I guess what brings me in is that I'm messing up a lot at work. I work in poultry processing right now. Which, honestly, is so gross. The smell just gets completely trapped in your hair. I actually bought this really expensive grapefruit clarifying shampoo to try and get it out, but it doesn't even work, and it was like thirty dollars at Sephora. I should probably just return it, but I lost the receipt. 

But anyway, my supervisor is getting really mad because I keep starting the sanitation steps, or like the batch logs and the end-of-line paperwork, and I somehow just... leave out the last parts. Like, every time. Even when I know my job completely depends on finishing them correctly, I just miss the end. Oh, and they just changed the brand of the pens we use for those logs, too, which is super annoying because the new ones smudge everywhere on the clipboard... but yeah, I just can't seem to finish the steps.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they fail to finish workplace duties, such as sanitation steps and paperwork, consistently leaving out the last parts.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions losing the receipt for the shampoo they bought.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, frequently going off on tangents about shampoo, Sephora, and the brand of pens used at work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had this kind of problem with paying attention or finishing tasks since you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, definitely. My mom actually still has my elementary school report cards, especially from around fourth grade. She keeps everything, honestly. Like, she has these massive plastic bins in her basement just stuffed with old macaroni art and spelling tests. I keep telling her she needs to scan them or something because the basement gets so damp, and last year they had that huge storm that flooded the neighbor's yard and completely ruined their riding lawnmower... 

But anyway, the report cards. They all basically said that I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork and turn in my homework. Like, I remember I would totally understand the lessons, but I'd just miss huge chunks of the instructions. Unless the teacher was literally standing right next to my desk. My fourth-grade teacher wore these really loud, clunky heels that you could hear echoing down the hall, so I always knew when she was walking over... but yeah, if she wasn't right there staying close to me, I'd just miss what I was supposed to be doing entirely.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes needing constant reminders to finish classwork, indicating difficulty sustaining attention on tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient notes missing huge chunks of instructions unless the teacher was standing right next to them, showing difficulty listening when spoken to.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they failed to finish classwork, turn in homework, and follow through on instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient's response demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, as they go off on tangents about their mother's basement, a flooded lawnmower, and their teacher's shoes.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel restless or have trouble sitting still?
turns.patient_response: Um, restless? Not really, no. I mean, I sit still just fine. I can sit for hours if I'm, like, looking at something on my phone or whatever. Actually, the other day I was sitting in the break room at work for so long my leg fell asleep. Have you ever had that happen where it's not just tingly, but it literally feels like a heavy block of wood? I tried to stand up to go back to the processing floor and I almost wiped out right in front of the vending machine. Which would have been so embarrassing because the guy who stocks it was there, and he's actually kind of cute, even though he wears this really aggressive cologne. It smells like, I don't know, pine needles and cheap body wash? But anyway, no, I don't really have trouble sitting still.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states she sits still just fine and can sit for hours, denying trouble remaining seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies feeling restless when asked directly.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have these same attention or follow-through problems outside of work, like at home or in other parts of your life?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, for sure. It's definitely not just at work. Like at home, my apartment is a total disaster right now. I keep meaning to clean it, and I'll start, like, doing the dishes, but then I'll see a piece of mail on the counter. And it's usually just junk mail, you know? Like those flyers for local pizza places. There's this one place down the street that keeps sending these super glossy menus with coupons, but their pizza is actually terrible. The crust is always soggy, and they never put enough cheese on it. I don't understand how they stay in business, honestly. I think it's because they're open until 3 AM and the college kids just order it when they're drunk. I used to do that when I was in undergrad, actually. My roommates and I would get it every Thursday night after going to this awful dive bar that had dollar well drinks... 

But yeah, I'll see the mail, and then I'll start sorting through it, and then I'll completely forget about the dishes. And the sink just fills up. It's really frustrating. So yeah, I guess it happens everywhere.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes starting chores, such as doing the dishes, but failing to finish them.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (a piece of mail) and goes off on a tangent of unrelated thoughts about pizza and college.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also tend to act impulsively, like interrupting people or blurting things out before you think?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really. I don't think I do that. I'm actually pretty quiet most of the time. Plus, at work, it's honestly so loud on the processing floor that you couldn't interrupt someone even if you tried. You have to practically scream to be heard over the machinery. We actually just got this brand new band saw on Tuesday, and it makes this awful, high-pitched whining sound. It sounds exactly like my roommate's cat when he's begging for his wet food. She buys him this ridiculously expensive organic salmon paté, which is so funny to me because I literally work with meat and fish all day, so I come home smelling like a butcher shop anyway. The cat is totally obsessed with me because of it. He just follows me around the apartment screaming until I finally go take a shower and wash it off... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, blurting things out. Yeah, no, I don't really have a problem with that. I mostly just keep my thoughts in my own head.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility in real-time by going off on a long tangent about a band saw and a cat, completely losing track of the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states they are 'pretty quiet most of the time,' denying excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting things out, stating they 'mostly just keep my thoughts in my own head.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient denies interrupting people, saying 'no, not really' in response to the doctor's specific question about it.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, were these attention or follow-through problems already present?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, I guess so. My mom actually still has all my old elementary school report cards in this big plastic tub in her basement. She's kind of a hoarder when it comes to that stuff. Like, she still has my macaroni art from kindergarten. But anyway, I was looking through them when I went home for Thanksgiving, and my fourth-grade teacher—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was? She always wore these really loud, chunky necklaces made out of wooden beads. They would clack against her desk when she leaned over. I always wondered where she bought them, maybe at some craft fair or something. My aunt makes jewelry like that, actually, but hers is mostly sea glass she finds on the beach. She lives out in Oregon now, right on the coast. It's beautiful out there, but it rains so much. I don't think I could handle that much rain. 

But yeah, on the report card, Mrs. Gable wrote that I was bright but I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork and turn in my homework. Like, I remember understanding the lessons just fine, but I would miss huge chunks of the instructions unless she was standing right next to my desk. So I guess it's been happening for a really long time.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly recalls needing constant reminders to finish classwork and turn in homework during elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic to discuss their teacher's necklaces, their aunt's jewelry, and the weather in Oregon before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel physically fidgety or like you need to move around when you’re supposed to stay still?
turns.patient_response:
Um, physically fidgety? No, I don't think so. I'm pretty okay with just sitting still. I mean, at work I'm standing for my whole shift anyway. We have these anti-fatigue mats on the floor, but honestly, by hour six, my feet are just killing me regardless. I bought these expensive insoles that were supposed to help, but they squeak every time I take a step. It drives my supervisor crazy. He's this really intense guy who used to be in the military, and he expects everything to run like clockwork. He actually yelled at me once because I was tapping my knife handle on the cutting board while I was waiting for the line to move. But that wasn't because I couldn't sit still, I was just bored. The conveyor belt broke down because someone dropped a whole tray of chicken breasts into the gears. It took maintenance like two hours to fish it all out, and the smell was... well, you can probably imagine. 

But yeah, anyway, no, I don't really feel like I have to move around or anything like that. I'm fine just staying put.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies feeling physically fidgety, despite mentioning a single instance of tapping a knife out of boredom.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they are 'pretty okay with just sitting still' and 'fine just staying put,' denying difficulty remaining seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies feeling a need to move around or feeling restless.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did these attention problems happen in more than one setting, like both at school and at home?
turns.patient_response:
Um, both at school and at home? I mean, I guess I don't really know for sure. I know my mom used to get so mad at me when I was little because my bedroom was always a complete disaster. Like, you couldn't even see the floor. I had this huge collection of those little plastic horses, you know the ones? They came with tiny little brushes and saddles that you always ended up losing in the carpet. I had like fifty of them, and I would set them up all over my room like they were grazing. My favorite one was this dapple gray one with a braided mane. I actually saw one just like it at a flea market last weekend. I almost bought it for nostalgia, but the guy wanted twenty bucks for it, which is crazy for a piece of plastic. I ended up buying a vintage Pyrex bowl instead. It’s that olive green color with the daisy pattern? I love cooking with vintage stuff, even though I mostly just make mac and cheese when I get home from the plant. I’m usually too tired to cook anything real after dealing with raw meat all day. 

But, um, what was the question? Oh, school and home. Yeah, I don't really know if it was the same kind of attention thing at home, or if I was just a messy kid. I just remember my mom yelling about my room a lot.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their childhood bedroom as 'always a complete disaster' where the floor wasn't visible, indicating difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls frequently losing the tiny brushes and saddles for their toy horses in the carpet.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about toy horses, a flea market, and vintage bowls.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient mentions being 'usually too tired to cook anything real' after a day of work.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient loses their train of thought and forgets the doctor's question mid-response ('what was the question?').

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child, were you often described as being very active or ‘always on the go’?
turns.patient_response:
Um, always on the go? No, I don't think anyone really described me like that. I was actually pretty quiet as a kid. I spent a lot of time just reading or drawing. I used to go to the library down the street from our house almost every day after school. The librarian there, Mrs. Higgins, she was so nice. She always saved the new fantasy books for me because she knew I loved them. She had this huge fluffy orange cat that used to sleep on the checkout counter. His name was Marmalade, which is kind of cliché, but it fit him perfectly. I tried to get a cat a couple of years ago, but it turns out my roommate is super allergic. Like, her eyes swell shut and everything. So we got a bearded dragon instead. His name is Spike. He's pretty cool, mostly just sits under his heat lamp all day and eats crickets. The crickets are kind of gross to deal with, honestly, especially when they escape and you hear them chirping behind the fridge at 2 AM. I had to pull the whole fridge out last month to catch one, and I found like three of my missing socks back there. I have no idea how they even got under there. 

But um, yeah, active as a kid? Not really. I was definitely more of a sit-in-the-corner-with-a-book kind of person.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions finding three of their 'missing socks' behind the fridge, indicating a tendency to lose items.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient goes on a long, rambling tangent about a librarian, various pets, and crickets, demonstrating distractibility through a chain of unrelated thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies being 'always on the go' or active as a child, stating they were quiet and preferred sitting with a book.
